I recently got a free membership to a gym through work. I have never been to gyms, but would like to start. Here is where I need help: I have trouble figuring out what activities to do, for how long, and how often. Basically, I would love it if somebody just told me what my workout was every day. Are there any books, apps, programs that can do this for me?

If you're going for cardio, I'd say get on the treadmill. Walk the first day. Bring a book. Listen to music. Watch TV. Just walk for a mile or so. 3.0 speed.

Next day, same distance, same speed, up the incline a little bit. 1-2 inclin

Next day, same distance. Faster speed. 3.5-4.0. Run a bit.

I think that's how I started. Walked most, ran some. Got used to it and started to run more, walk some. Then I'd get lazy and just end up walking at the max incline (it hurts).

Just up either distance, speed, and/or incline a little bit each day as you get more and more used to it.

edit- You can try the Kilimanjaro mode on the elliptical. I think it's done after you succeed and finish the "hill". It's a fun mode... til it hurts.

What exactly are your goals with regard to fitness? Are you trying get strong, look good, just stay healthy, etc? There's a lot of different things you can do at the gym but we can't recommend a plan unless we know what you want out of it.

I am mostly looking to lose fat and be healthy. I have gained about 40 lbs over the past two years, and I would like to take it back off again. I am married, so looking fit would be nice, but is not critical. Strength is irrelevant.

Losing weight is 80% diet. I lost 20lbs when I started college and I did pretty much no exercise other than walking around campus; I just ate less. I suggest calculating your TDEE to see how much you need to eat to maintain your current weight and then eating 250 to 500 calories less to lose. You will also definitely need to keep track of your food intake using an app like MyFitnessPal.

As for looking fit, you could consider lifting. I really like Ice Cream Fitness as a beginner lifting routine; other Voaters might be able to different routines. Gaining muscle will also help you lose weight faster and keep you from getting skinny fat.

Whether or not you want to do cardio is up to you. I personally think its important for heart health and like to do cardio on my ''off-days'' from lifting, but it's not necessary for losing weight. I usually swim or take my gym's zumba classes. Since you have access to a gym you can explore what machines or classes you like best.

Overall your routine might look like:

Monday: Weight Training

Tuesday: 30 - 40 min Cardio

Wednesday: Weight training

Thursday: 30 - 40min Cardio

Friday: Weight training

Saturday & Sunday: Either cardio one day and rest next, or take both days off
I can vouch for Ice Cream Fitness. I made amazing progress on that program with a good diet.

Some good apps to start: C25K, and StrongLifts.

Couch to 5k takes you from zero conditioning to running for 30 minutes straight. I would recommend it to anyone who is healthy enough to run. If running isn't your thing you can check out the exercise bikes. Or even the aerobics classes. Some gyms have insanity and Zumba classes which look fun. Maybe yoga or Pilates? It's up to you.

StrongLifts is all about weight training and the app is literally a list of lifts to check off, then it tells you how long to rest, then more lifts. It tells you what to do and links to videos on how to do it. The types of lifts it starts you on can seem intimidating to a beginner though.

To me the most effective quick and enjoyable way to maintain a healthy body is to learn and progress compound lifts ( squats, deadlifts, power cleans, etc)

Learning them can be tricky on your own... if your gym's trainers won't show you then you might just have to watch videos about form.

I'll be happy to answer any questions you might have!

This is one of those stories that makes one think that conspiracy theories and conspiracy's in general are real.

One of the biggest tells of Stuxnet was that computers (PLCs that don't run Windows or Linux) that were isolated from the internet, could indeed be compromised. The other biggie was that actual physical damage in the real world (not just damaging computer code on a computer) - was absolutely doable. So it's one of the first documented weaponised malwares.
Any computer/electrical engineer could have told you it was possible. The thing is, it is usually assumed that it is not worth the effort. No company can afford to shield themselves against that.

Simply saying something is possible (which had already been occurring for several years) versus actually accomplishing it, is what set Stuxnet apart.

To say that no company can afford to shield themselves against attack means to throw in the proverbial towel. It means that Big Data is then to be the property of anybody and everybody. This would not be anything of interest to capital investors. No public or private companies are saying defense isn't worth the effort - it would be commercial suicide.

The fact that offense is currently winning, is where computer security sits right now. Every Gov't is doing it to some extent or another, and for many it is a full court press.

Will the next phase be not one of Gov'ts but of commercial companies tussling for advantage?

Sorry, but there is no way to defend against a a virus similar to stuxnet. It was extremely well hidden, modified things at a very low level that are not physically perceptible.

The ONLY reason it was ever discovered was that there was a problem in it that caused a certain computer to continually reboot. The only other way they could have detected it would have been to measure the frequency through another mean than the controller itself.

To even think that ANY company is trying to shield themselves against such attack is wishful thinking. Even the military could not have shielded themselves against it.
